metadata.title: Significance of Methyltransferase-like 5 Expression in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

sections.text: Objectives Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a malignant tumour with high-local invasiveness and lymph node metastasis potential. It is associated with poor prognosis and postoperative cosmetic complications. Therefore, developing molecular targets for early detection, diagnosis, and treatment is imperative. Methyltransferase-like 5 (METTL5), a newly identified N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification writer, has been shown to exhibit tumour-promoting functions in several cancers. However, the significance of METTL5 expression in OSCC remains unexplored. Methods In this study, we performed gene expression and in silico analyses of METTL5 and related molecules using publicly available datasets. The clinicopathological significance of METTL5 was assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in 62 OSCC specimens. Results Analysis of public databases revealed that METTL5 expression was highly elevated in head and neck SCC. Genes related to METTL5, including TP53RK-binding protein ( TPRKB ) and ZZ-type zinc finger and EF-hand domain protein 1 ( ZZEF1 ), were identified. Furthermore, METTL5 expression levels were positively correlated with those of ferroptosis-related genes. IHC analysis revealed that METTL5 expression was associated with local tumour progression ( P = .0367). Multivariate analysis revealed that METTL5 expression is associated with poor prognosis for overall survival ( P = .0376). Conclusions Our results suggest that METTL5 may serve as a new diagnostic and therapeutic target for OSCC.

Head and neck cancer, including oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), is the sixth most common cancer worldwide. Approximately 59,660 new cases and 12,770 deaths were expected across the United States in 2025. 1 OSCC exhibits high-local invasiveness and lymph node metastasis. It is often detected at an advanced stage and has a poor 5-year survival rate despite the remarkable advances in molecular biology and oncology in recent years. 2 Postoperative functional and aesthetic impairments are also major issues, necessitating early detection and treatment. However, no useful diagnostic markers have been identified for OSCC, and only a few effective drugs, such as cetuximab and pembrolizumab, are available. 3 Therefore, molecular diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies targeting OSCC need to be urgently developed. RNA methylation refers to the addition of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) to mRNA after transcription. This process is crucial for embryonic development, neurogenesis, cell self-renewal, and tumorigenesis by regulating gene expression. 4 This chemical modification is reversible and requires writers, such as methyltransferase-like proteins 3 (METTL3) and METTL14, that read modification information and identify fat mass and obesity-related (FTO) proteins. Moreover, demethylases, such as α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase alkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5), act as erasers, and RNA readers, such as YT521-B homology domain-containing proteins (eg, YTHDF and YTHDC), recognise modifications. 5 Generally, chemical modification of m6A often has tumour-promoting effects. Previously, we reported that elevated m6A levels in OSCC are positively correlated with advanced clinical stage, lymph node metastasis, and venous invasion, and that expression of a novel m6A writer, vir-like m6A methyltransferase-associated (VIRMA), was associated with poor prognosis. 6 Studies have shown that m6A may also function as a tumour suppressor, 5 , 7 playing a dual role. However, the definitive role of m6A in cancer remains unclear. The METTL family has 33 members, all of which contain an S-adenosylmethionine binding domain. 8 Among these molecules, METTL5 is a newly discovered m6A writer, 5 which adds the m6A 1832 mark to the eukaryotic 18S ribosomal subunit, enhancing RNA binding. 9 Studies have shown that METTL5 can promote cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis, and mismatch repair. 8 METTL5 has been reported to exhibit tumour-promoting activity in breast, 10 lung, 7 and gastrointestinal cancer. 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 Additionally, METTL5 can suppress ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death induced by lipid oxidation products, in several malignancies. 14 , 15 Since cancer cells contain abundant iron ions, ferroptosis has attracted attention as a novel cancer treatment strategy. 16 However, the relationship between METTL5 and ferroptosis in OSCC remains unclear. As RNA methylation is independent of genetic abnormalities, it may be responsible for carcinogenesis and cancer heterogeneity that cannot be explained by known genetic mutations. 5 , 17 Therefore, understanding RNA methylation may help elucidate the complex mechanisms underlying cancer and facilitate the development of novel cancer treatments. The METTL family offers promise as molecular targets for cancer therapy. 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 Therefore, we investigated METTL5 expression and its potential role in OSCC in this study.

sections.section: Public Database And In Silico Analyses
sections.text: Gene expression data were obtained from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ) and analysed using Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis 2 web server ( https://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn/ ) and TNMplot ( https://tnmplot.com/analysis/ ). This database contains clinical information for 528 patients, including 382 (72.4%) with oral cancer, 116 (22%) with laryngeal cancer, and 30 (5.6%) with oropharyngeal cancer. It also includes RNA-seq data from 519 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) who were followed up for 30 days or more, and 40 healthy subjects. 25 , 26 All gene expression levels by RNA-seq in the database are transcripts per million (TPM) normalised. Further, in silico analysis was performed using Linkedomics ( https://www.linkedomics.org/ ). 27

In this study, we used formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens from 62 patients with confirmed diagnosis of OSCC (mean aged: 70 years; age range: 29-91 years) who visited the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Kagoshima University Hospital, Kagoshima, Japan, from 2014 to 2016. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed on all 62 specimens. Of these, m6A could be quantified in 36 specimens. Tumour stage and histological grade were determined according to the Union for International Cancer Control TNM classification system (8th edition) and World Health Organization criteria, respectively. Medical records were obtained from the patient database managed by the hospital. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Kagoshima University, Kagoshima, Japan (approval number: 213223-1).

The m6A modification levels of total RNA were quantified using the EpiQuik m6A RNA Methylation Quantitation Kit (Epigentek) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 200 ng of total RNA was bound to each well, and m6A levels were quantified colourimetrically using antibodies with a method similar to an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm. 6

IHC was performed on 3-μm-thick consecutive sections obtained from each block. After deparaffinization, endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with methanol containing 0.3% H 2 O 2 for 30 minutes. For antigen retrieval, the sections were soaked in tris-ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid buffer and microwaved for 1 hour. The specimens were treated with protein-blocking serum for 10 minutes to block nonspecific antibody interactions. Then, they were incubated with anti-METTL5 primary antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology), diluted to 0.5 mg/mL, for 8 hours at 4°C, followed by horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (Medical & Biological Laboratories), diluted to 0.5%, for 1 hour at room temperature. Colour development and counterstaining were performed using diaminobenzidine (DAB) solution (DAKO) and Mayer’s haematoxylin (Sigma-Aldrich), respectively.

METTL5 immunostaining was evaluated using proportional and intensity scores, as previously reported. 6 The proportionality score was based on the percentage of immune-positive cells and classified as 0: 0%; (1) 1% to 10%; (2) 11% to 35%; (3) 36% to 70%; and (4) 71% to 100%. The intensity score was based on immunostaining intensity and was classified as 0 (negative), 1 (weak), 2 (moderate), or 3 (strong). METTL5 immunoreactivity was defined as a total score of 5 or higher, calculated by summing the proportionality and intensity scores (range: 0-7).

Statistical analyses were performed using Fisher’s exact, Welch’s t-, and unpaired t-tests. Disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were analysed using the Kaplan–Meier method. Inter-group comparisons were conducted using the log-rank test. Multivariate analysis of prognosis was performed using the Cox proportional hazards model. All statistical analyses were conducted using JMP 13 (SAS Institute). P -values < .05 were considered statistically significant.

sections.section: Gene Expression Analysis Of Mettl5 In Hnscc
sections.text: First, we compared METTL5 expression levels with those of the tRNA methyltransferase activator subunit 11-2 ( TRMT112 ) in 519 HNSCC and 44 normal oral tissues using the TCGA database. METTL5 expression levels were higher in the HNSCC tissues than in the normal tissues ( Figure 1 A). Furthermore, HNSCC cases with high METTL5 expression had worse DFS ( P = .021; Figure 1 B) and OS ( P = .011; Figure 1 C) than those with low METTL5 expression levels (cut-off points, 60%). Figure 2 A depicts a heatmap of genes that were positively and negatively correlated with METTL5 expression in this dataset. Functional gene set enrichment analysis based on gene ontology revealed that several genes associated with METTL5 were enriched for mitochondrial function, RNA binding and maintenance ( Figure 2 B).

Among the METTL5 -related genes mentioned above, we further analysed those encoding TP53RK-binding protein (TPRKB) and ZZ-type zinc finger and EF-hand domain protein 1 (ZZEF1). TPRKB is associated with threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification of tRNA and loss of TP53 function, 28 while ZZEF1 has only been reported to participate in histone methylation and acetylation. 29 Incidentally, little is known about the exact roles of both genes in cancer. The expression of TPRKB was significantly higher ( P < .0001; Figure 3 A), whereas that of ZZEF1 was much lower ( P < .0001; Figure 3 D) in the HNSCC group. Patients with high TPRKB expression had significantly lower DFS ( P = .015; Figure 3 B), whereas those with high ZZEF1 expression had a favourable prognosis for OS ( P = .0066; Figure 3 F). However, TPRKB and ZZEF1 expression were not associated with OS ( Figure 3 C) and DFS ( Figure 3 E). Incidentally, the cutoff points for gene expression levels of ZZEF1 and TPRKB are 65% and 60%, respectively.

sections.section: Correlation Between Mettl5 Expression And That Of Vegf- And Ferroptosis-Related Genes
sections.text: Previously, we showed that m6A expression was higher in OSCC cases with venous invasion. 6 Hence, we investigated the relationship between METTL5 expression and that of the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) family, which is most relevant to angiogenesis in OSCC. 30 VEGFA expression levels were positively correlated with those of METTL5 ( P = .053, Figure 4 A), although the difference was not statistically significant. METTL5 expression was significantly correlated with that of VEGFC ( P = .0046, Figure 4 B). However, there was no association between METTL5 and VEGFD ( Figure 4 C). METTL5 is known to promote ferroptosis resistance in cancer. 14 , 15 Consistently, we found that the METTL 5 expression levels were positively correlated with those of ferroptosis-related molecules GPX4 ( P < .000, Figure 4 D), SLC7A11 ( P < .0001, Figure 4 E), and NFE2L2 ( P < .0001, Figure 4 F).

sections.section: Expression Of Mettl5 In Oscc Specimens
sections.text: Next, immunostaining analysis of METTL5 expression using 62 OSCC cases revealed positive nuclear or cytoplasmic staining in the OSCC specimens, whereas no expression was detected in normal oral mucosa ( Figure 5 A). Specifically, 28/62 specimens (45.2%) were found to express METTL5. Table 1 summarises the relationship between METTL5 expression and clinicopathologic features. In OSCC cases, METTL5 was more frequently expressed in sites other than the tongue ( P = .0050). Further, METTL5 expression was significantly correlated with T grade ( P = .0367). METTL5 was positive in 63.6% (14/22) of T3 and T4 cases, whereas only 35% (14/40) of Tis to T2 cases exhibited METTL5 expression. No other clinicopathological factors were associated with METTL5 expression. Subsequently, we examined the relationship between m6A and METTL5 expression in the 36 cases in which m6A was quantified. We found that cases expressing METTL5 (0.5841 ± 0.4000) had significantly higher m6A levels than those without METTL5 expression (0.2978 ± 0.2482, P = .0304).

We next investigated the association between METTL5 expression and OS (22-2298 days) and DFS (12-2237 days) in patients with OSCC using Kaplan–Meier analysis. During the follow-up, 19 patients died, and 24 patients had local or metastatic recurrence of OSCC. Although the DFS rate tended to be lower in METTL5-positive cases compared with METTL5-negative cases, this difference was not statistically significant ( Figure 5 C, P = .1589). However, the OS of METTL5-positive patients ( Figure 5 D, P = .0254) was significantly shorter than that of METTL5-negative patients. Finally, we performed a multivariate analysis using the Cox proportional hazards model, including T stages, clinical stages, lymph node metastasis, and METTL5 expression as confounding factors for OSCC prognosis. The results showed that only METTL5 expression was an independent predictor of poor prognosis for patients with OSCC ( P = .0376, Table 2 ), but not for DFS.

METTL5 is a novel m6A modification writer that has been shown to exhibit tumour-promoting activity. 7 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 In this study, we analysed the significance of METTL5 expression by performing IHC on FFPE specimens obtained from patients with OSCC. METTL5 expression levels were higher in OSCC than in normal mucosal tissues, with higher expression in advanced cases. METTL5 acts as an independent poor prognostic factor for OS. In silico analysis using big data revealed that several genes associated with METTL5 are related to mitochondria or RNA binding. Among these, TPRKB and ZZEF1 showed positive and negative correlations with METTL5 expression, respectively. TPRKB is known to promote the progression of liver cancer, 31 while ZZEF1 regulates transcriptional activity by binding to the histone H3 tail. 29 However, the roles of both proteins in cancer remain unknown. To our knowledge, this is the first report to show that TPRKB and ZZEF1 are positively and negatively correlated with HNSCC prognosis, respectively. In our ongoing work, we are examining their functions and roles in OSCC. Furthermore, the detailed relationship between METTL5 and other mitochondria-related molecules or RNA-binding proteins should be clarified. Previously, we showed that high m6A levels in OSCC may be associated with venous invasion and that the expression of a novel methyltransferase, VIRMA, indicates poor prognosis. 6 In this study, we found that METLL5-expressing cases exhibited elevated m6A levels. We also demonstrated a significant correlation between METLL5 expression levels and those of VEGFA / VEGFC . In addition to promoting angiogenesis, VEGFC is a potent lymphangiogenic factor in OSCC. 30 Recent reports have shown that elevated METTL5 levels suppress tumour immunity 32 as well as enhance proliferative and invasive potential by activating c-myc 33 in OSCC. However, the association between METTL5 and VEGF signalling in cancer has not yet been demonstrated. The relationship between METTL5 expression and tumour microenvironment, including angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis, also remains to be elucidated. METTL5 has been shown to promote ferroptosis resistance in cancer. 14 , 15 Ferroptosis, a type of cell death distinct from apoptosis, is induced in an iron ion-dependent manner. Several types of cancers are known to be ferroptosis-resistant. 16 While ferroptosis contributes to tumour growth by suppressing tumour immunity and increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, elevated levels of iron ions and ROS induce ferroptosis, exerting tumour-suppressive effects. Therefore, ferroptosis acts as a double-edged sword in cancer. 34 Although the molecular mechanism of ferroptosis is quite complex, GPX4, an essential enzyme that prevents lipid peroxidation, has been shown to protect cells from ferroptosis. NFE2L2 regulates oxidative stress-related genes, including GPX4 , making it an important defence mechanism against ferroptosis. 16 Furthermore, SLC7A11 converts cystine to cysteine, providing resistance to ferroptosis by protecting cells from oxidative stress. 35 In this study, bioinformatics analysis of the TCGA database revealed that METTL5 expression in OSCC is positively correlated with that of ferroptosis-related molecules, including GPX4, SLC7A11 , and NFE2L2 . Furthermore, METTL5 knockdown reduced the expression levels of these ferroptosis-related genes in OSCC cells. Inducing ferroptosis in cancer cells may be an effective strategy to selectively kill these cells without harming surrounding normal cells. Furthermore, ferroptosis-inducing therapy by suppressing GPX4 has shown promising results in animal models. 36 Drugs that inhibit cystine uptake, such as sulfasalazine, erastin, and sorafenib, are potential therapeutic candidates for targeting SLC7A11 and inducing ferroptosis. 37 HG106, an SLC7A11 inhibitor, has already been developed. 38 Cancer cells resistant to existing anticancer drugs are highly sensitive to ferroptosis, making it a promising therapeutic target. 16 , 39 In the future, we aim to develop a METTL5-targeted ferroptosis-inducing therapy for OSCC. Regarding the METTL family as a direct therapeutic target for cancer, several METTL3 inhibitors have been reported. 21 For example, the small-molecule inhibitor STM2457 suppresses acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) development 23 and medulloblastoma progression 24 by blocking METTL3 expression. The METTL3 inhibitor UZH1a has been shown to reduce m6A mRNA levels, promote apoptosis, and induce cell cycle arrest in specific cancer cell lines, 20 thereby inhibiting tumour growth and extending survival in glioma mouse models. 19 Furthermore, eltrombopag, which targets METTL3 and METTL14, effectively reduces m6A modification levels in AML cell lines and inhibits proliferation. 18 Additionally, clinical trials of STC-15, an orally administered small-molecule METTL3 inhibitor, are underway in patients with advanced solid tumours. 22 However, as METTL3-mediated m6A modification plays an important regulatory role in the central nervous system, systemic administration of METTL3 inhibitors warrants further investigation. 21 Although inhibitors targeting METTL family members other than METTL3 have not yet been developed, scutellarin, a compound extracted from Scutellaria barbata , has been shown to suppress METTL5 expression and exert antitumor effects in ovarian cancer. 40 Recently, METTL5 -knockout mouse embryonic stem cells were shown to exhibit reduced expression of pluripotency molecules, such as KLF transcription factor 4 (Klf4), Nanog, and SRY-box transcription factor 2 (SOX2), and diminished differentiation potential, particularly in the neuroectodermal and mesodermal lineages. 41 These data suggest that METTL5 is closely associated with pluripotency and differentiation. Since eradicating cancer stem cells is directly linked to cancer control, anticancer therapies targeting METTL5 might prove useful. However, METTL5 -deficient mice were shown to exhibit reduced viability, weight loss, ocular and craniofacial abnormalities, intellectual disability, and hyperactivity. 8 , 41 Further research is needed to assess its clinical applicability as a molecular-targeted drug with minimal side effects in cancer treatment.

This study revealed that METTL5 functions as an m6A writer and is involved in the progression and prognosis of OSCC. In recent years, molecular biological findings of OSCC have been emerging, such as the discovery that seryl-tRNA synthetase (SARS1) is a therapeutic target for OSCC. 42 and that SRY-box11 (SOX11) and GLIS family zinc finger 2 (GLIS2) are useful biomarkers for predicting the progression of oral leukoplakia to OSCC. 43 Although many challenges remain, large-scale clinical studies, detailed cutting-edge in vitro research, and in vivo treatment experiments are urgently needed to develop new diagnostic and therapeutic systems targeting METTL5 in OSCC.
